I grew up in the Midwest in an area with many small farms. I’ve done a little gardening and preserving, and I’ve known many hunters, fishermen, and people who embraced rural self sufficiency. I’ll share a few thoughts as you get started on your new lifestyle.

You'll need to find the right balance for yourself between casual rural pursuits, sustainability or profitability of your 3 acre parcel. Others can better advise how to maximize profit if that's your goal. If you're looking for privacy and a few nice rural pursuits, you'll get lots of good advice. Many of the ideas you'll get will be very labor intensive. That's the nature of homesteading. You'll get more great ideas than you'll have time to implement properly, so be selective and remember it won't all get done the first year. It’s not a purity test. Start small and keep a journal so you don’t repeat mistakes and can keep track of the adjustments you intend to make next season.

Look to Eastern Europe during the dark days of the Cold War, or for that matter, US victory gardens. Anyone who had a patch of dirt to call their own had a few fruit trees and bushes, a little veggie and herb garden, maybe some bees. Cold frames or greenhouses extended the season. If they could, they raised a few chickens and rabbits for protein. They were very efficient in how they used their space. The same is probably true of Japan. I'm not familiar with farming in Japan, but as an island culture, they are extremely thrifty with the use of both indoor and outdoor spaces.

With a little effort and the cooperation of weather, you can produce a lot of food, but it is seasonal. Plan for not only raising the food, but also preserving and storing it for winter. You can also sell it, but of course your crops will be abundant at the same time as everyone else in your area. You won't get far selling excess zucchini in the summer. Canning is great for preservation. It requires many containers and adequate storage space, as well as a concerted effort to get the canning done as produce ripens. The containers are re-useable and readily available. Canned food is marketable. Check out any food regulations, especially kitchen requirements for your state. Usually labeling food as 'organic' involves a mess of regulations. It can be easier to raise food organically and not label it that way. If you sell locally you can explain it to customers. Our local CSA farm is like that. Freezing is easier to execute but requires ongoing energy use and is at risk if you have an outage. I prefer frozen meat to canned, but you have to watch for freezer burn and be sure you have backup power. Dehydration is excellent for many foods. I do it on a small scale, especially with root veggies or mushrooms, or even jerky. It permits you to store a lot of food in a small space with no ongoing energy cost.

Farm animals add another layer of planning and responsibility. I'd love to have some chickens, as some people in our suburb now do. We also like to travel, and my husband rightly points out that we'd need a chicken sitter. Then there are the hawks. So we don't have chickens – or even a cat. Whatever animals you keep need to be fed, vetted, sheltered, perhaps sheared, milked, slaughtered, butchered, processed, etc. Think it through in terms of your lifestyle before you buy them. Somebody has to be able to provide backup if you're sick or want to travel - even for a weekend. That's a big consideration if you have any livestock requiring milking. There's a reason you don't see dairy farmers taking a lot of vacations.

As you think about your dwelling, you need to consider the extreme weather conditions in your area. If you're in a place where tornadoes, hurricanes, or flash floods are an issue, you need to secure appropriate shelter for yourself and loved ones. That might mean underground shelter, roof strapping, elevation, etc. The semi-permanent house on a trailer bed might offer great tax advantages, but be sure you have adequate storm protection suited to your area. An underground shelter could serve as storm protection, root cellar and canned food storage.
